subject: chemistry-2
question: What is the primary purpose of the mole concept in chemistry?

options.text: It links a countable number of particles to a mass that can be measured on a laboratory balance
It converts the volume of a liquid sample into its density without any mass measurement
It fixes the number of atoms written as subscripts when a chemical formula is constructed
It sets the volume that one mole of any liquid occupies, so samples can be compared by volume

explanation:
Substances react in whole-number particle ratios, yet no balance can count individual particles. The mole is the conversion bridge: molar mass turns a weighable mass into a particle count, so 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate (100.09 g/mol) corresponds to a measurable 25.02 g and to about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units. This macroscopic-to-microscopic link underpins stoichiometry, solution concentration, and clinical dosage calculations. Subscripts come from bonding and charge balance, and molar volume is a separate concept that applies mainly to gases.

ELI-10: You cannot count grains of rice before dinner, but you can weigh out a cup and know approximately how many you have. Chemists face the same problem in a harsher form, since atoms are far too small to count at all. So they weigh instead, and molar mass is the conversion card: one mole of this substance weighs this many grams. Need 0.25 mol of chalk? Weigh 25.02 g and you have counted about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units without counting anything.
